document.title: 11 September: The Plot and the Plotters (CTC 2003-40044HC)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Central Intelligence Agency 9/11 File: Hundreds of Secret Agency Documents on Osama Bin Laden Declassified

key_claims: KSM, uncle of Ramzi Yousef, was a chief planner of the 11 September attacks and supported the 1993 WTC bombing.
Bin Ladin reportedly approved the plot in 1998 and al-Qa'ida leaders selected the operatives.
The three Hamburg pilots were recruited in Germany and supported by a Hamburg al-Qa'ida network.
Al-Hazmi and al-Mihdhar were al-Qa'ida veterans who fought in Bosnia and Afghanistan.
Most remaining hijackers were young Saudis from southwest Saudi Arabia radicalized locally.
Nineteen hijackers spent time in al-Qa'ida camps in Afghanistan in late 1999-2001, often routing through other countries.
Bin Ladin personally selected the targets and the five initial pilot candidates, and Atta was chosen senior coordinator after the Kandahar meetings.
After the Ramadan 1999 meetings, Atta had no direct contact with al-Qa'ida leadership, and instructions passed through intermediaries such as Bin al-Shibh.
The Kuala Lumpur and Bangkok meetings in January 2000 brought together al-Mihdhar, al-Hazmi, and USS Cole planner Khallad.
The UAE served as a key financial hub, with funds reaching Atta and al-Shehhi directly or via Bin al-Shibh and Motassadeq.
CIA and FBI are increasingly skeptical that Atta met Iraqi intelligence officer al-Ani in Prague in April 2001.
The hijackers used a Westernized appearance and clean records to enter and live in the US undetected.
In July 2001 Atta and Bin al-Shibh met in Spain, and Atta had control over final target selection and timing.
The attack date was relayed from Atta via Bin al-Shibh and KSM to Bin Ladin.
Funds for the plot flowed through intermediaries via UAE, Germany and the US, and unused funds were returned to al-Qa'ida in early September 2001.
Al-Hazmi and al-Mihdhar were early al-Qa'ida-linked extremists, having fought in Bosnia and sworn loyalty to Bin Ladin.
The Hamburg pilots may have been recruited in Germany; Zammar was a common acquaintance of Atta's circle.
Bin al-Shibh shifted to a financial and communications intermediary role after failing to enter the US.
Atta, al-Shehhi and Jarrah may have been recruited in Germany, unlike other hijackers.
The 12 Saudi muscle hijackers joined the plot later than the pilots.
Hijackers were selected for operational and political value; many came from 'Asir, where Bin Ladin's family roots lie.
Personal and family ties, including two sets of brothers, were important to the network.
Al-Ghamdis and others claimed to travel to Chechnya but probably went to Afghanistan.
Several hijackers reportedly trained at camps in Afghanistan before arriving in the US.
Beirut-Tehran was a customary route for al-Qa'ida members traveling to Afghanistan.
Al-Shehhi handled much of the logistics and some financing; Banihammad played a significant financial role.
Hamburg was where Atta, al-Shehhi and Jarrah formed ties.
Al-Mihdhar and al-Hazmi fought in Bosnia and then met a known al-Qa'ida operative in Malaysia.
All 19 hijackers spent time in Afghanistan camps, presumably receiving general al-Qa'ida training.
The 9/11 attacks were conceived after Bin Ladin's 1998 declaration of jihad against the US.
The first wave leadership cadre arrived in 2000; the second wave muscle hijackers arrived in spring and summer 2001.
Al-Mihdhar and al-Hazmi fought in Bosnia and met al-Qa'ida operative Walid Ba Attash in Malaysia in January 2000.
Hijackers wired leftover funds to Mustafa Ahmed in UAE just before the attacks.
Salim al-Hazmi fought for the Taliban against the Northern Alliance before joining the plot.
